item.title: A Model-Theoretic Formalization of AlKhwaremis ilm alfaraid
item.description: arXiv:2610.33629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a model theoretic and computational formalization of AlKhwarizmis treatment of inheritance within the framework of Computational Fiqh. We first show that every inheritance configuration in a specified class is representable as a finite system of rational linear equalities and inequalities, and that such systems are decided exactly by Fourier Motzkin elimination over Q. We then define the fixed dimensional inheritance structure Vd with distinguished claimant coordinates, and prove that every admissible rational linear coordinate realization is isomorphic to Vd, this establishes the algebraic representation as canonical within that class. The complete first order theory Td of Vd is shown to be complete by construction and is explicitly distinguished from the decidability of the inheritance relevant fragment. The methodological principle is then related to a broader formalization of closed Fiqh domains via exhaustive case generation, Horn clause axiomatization, and terminating deduction, yielding domain relative computational completeness.
item.dc:creator: Elnaserledinellah Mahmoud Abdelwahab

item.title: Unit: a type checker for dependent type theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.34264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Unit, a type checker for dependent type theory with a module system in the tradition of Automath and a uniform treatment of definitions: two uses of a definition are compared by name and arguments before anything is unfolded, and otherwise the definition declared last is opened. There is no unification, no instance search, no tactics and no unfolding heuristic, so the work of checking can be observed and compared with the informal proof. With Unit we have checked a model of univalent type theory, synthetic algebraic geometry up to Ch\^atelet's theorem, and synthetic Stone duality with its cohomology. These developments show that a small, uniform system supports substantial mathematics, and give concrete reasons to reconsider the complexity routinely accepted in proof assistants.
item.dc:creator: Thierry Coquand

item.title: A Lambda Calculus Based on Quantum Logic
item.description: arXiv:2610.34266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a typed lambda calculus based on quantum logic. We first present a natural deduction system for quantum logic with the Sasaki hook as its implication operation and then formulate a typed lambda calculus connected to this system through the Curry-Howard correspondence. We prove soundness and completeness of the former with respect to orthomodular lattices and strong normalization of the latter. The resulting lambda calculus has the characteristic feature that only one assumption is available in the typing derivation that serves as the premise of $\lambda$-abstraction. Under this restriction, ordinary currying is not available in general, but it is still possible to perform $\lambda$-abstraction by combining multiple assumptions into a single argument of product type and to construct a term corresponding to a deduction using the Sasaki projection.
item.dc:creator: Kenji Tokuo

item.title: Vector space embeddings of modal logic formulas: theory and application
item.description: arXiv:2610.34327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning tasks over modal logics are notoriously difficult, comprising problems which are often semi-decidable. Hence, it is not rare for applications leveraging such tasks to exploit heuristic approaches able to give results in an acceptable amount of time, at the cost of some inaccuracies. Some approaches may benefit from vector embeddings, allowing for instance to involve neural networks and machine learning models in the reasoning process. This work aims at providing a new way to provide such embeddings specifically for the modal case, aiming for faster reasoning through both mathematical and learning techniques.
item.dc:creator: Pietro Casavecchia, Alberto Paparella, Leonardo Serrentino

item.title: Proceedings Twelfth International Conference on Non-Classical Logics. Theory and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.34489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Classical Logics. Theory and Applications (NCL) is an international conference aimed at presenting novel results and survey papers in the broad field of non-classical logics and their applications. The first two editions were held in {\L}{\'o}d{\'z}, Poland, in September 2008 and 2009. Subsequent editions were organised in Toru{\'n} (2010, 2012, 2015, 2018) and {\L}{\'o}d{\'z} (2011, 2013, 2016, 2022, 2024). The tenth edition of the conference, organised by the University of {\L}{\'o}d{\'z} in 2022, was the first to have its proceedings published in EPTCS. We are honoured and pleased to continue this practice and, for the third time, include all accepted long papers in an EPTCS volume. Furthermore, for the first time, we have also included all accepted extended abstracts in the volume.
item.dc:creator: Andrzej Indrzejczak (University of {\L}{\'o}d{\'z}, Poland), Tomasz Jarmu{\.z}ek (Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toru{\'n}, Poland), Mateusz Klonowski (Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toru{\'n}, Poland), Micha{\l} Zawidzki (University of {\L}{\'o}d{\'z}, Poland)

item.title: Connecting Quantum Proof Systems and Hoare Logic
item.description: arXiv:2610.34723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifying quantum programs today requires specialized proof systems built on interactive theorem provers such as Rocq, Lean, Isabelle, or Why3, and even modest quantum algorithms cost substantial human effort to verify. Because quantum programs cannot be effectively checked by runtime testing, formal verification is the only viable path to correctness, making the cost of these bespoke systems the chief barrier to scalable quantum software assurance. We show that verifying a quantum program should be no harder than verifying a classical array program, a paradigm commonly used in parallel programming: the Qafny quantum proof system translates into Hoare logic with array theory completely (every Qafny proof becomes a valid Hoare triple) and soundly (a valid translated triple certifies only true quantum specifications), and we mechanize the completeness direction in Rocq. The embedding determinizes quantum proof obligations and exposes the full machinery of classical automated verifiers (e.g. Dafny and SMT-based separation logic) to quantum code, removing the need for dedicated quantum proof system infrastructure. In particular, the embedding supplies the correctness argument that the existing compilation of Qafny into Dafny lacks.
item.dc:creator: Liyi Li, Zoukarneini Difaizi Tagba, Alex Potanin

item.title: Unbelievably Complex
item.description: arXiv:2610.35106v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the directed simplicial complex: this is an extension of a simplicial complex with a direction on its faces. This enables us to model a local notion of belief in a three-valued semantics, in which formulas may be true, false, or undefined. Of particular interest is a class of directed simplicial complexes called cups, in which any maximal set of vertices of different colors is a facet. Cups permit a more concise relational representation. We give examples and applications of our logical semantics. We then provide a sound and complete axiomatization for the class of directed simplicial complexes and extend it to an axiomatization for the class of cups. We include a detailed technical comparison with other works on belief on complexes. Our work generalizes a prior axiomatization for knowledge on (undirected) impure simplicial complexes.
item.dc:creator: Hans van Ditmarsch, Djanira Gomes, Rojo Randrianomentsoa, Thomas Studer

item.title: Formal Explanations for Linear Temporal Logic over Finite Traces
item.description: arXiv:2610.35169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear Temporal Logic over Finite Traces (LTLf) is widely used in Artificial Intelligence to specify desired temporal behavior and determine whether finite traces satisfy or violate it. Explaining these outcomes is essential for debugging and trust. However, existing approaches typically capture either sufficient reasons or counterfactual causes, without clarifying their relationship. We introduce a native characterization of abductive (AXps) and contrastive (CXps) explanations directly over finite traces, based on locking and unlocking time-indexed events. We prove its equivalence to the classifier-based formulation, and show that CXps coincide with a recently proposed temporal causality semantics for LTLf. This characterization enables an efficient implementation based on the enumeration of minimal unsatisfiable cores and minimal correction sets of ASP programs. Experiments on real-world event logs demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.
item.dc:creator: Valeria Fionda, Antonio Ielo, Francesco Ricca

item.title: Quantitative Reachability Properties Beyond Decisiveness
item.description: arXiv:2610.35308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decisiveness is central to reachability algorithms for infinite Markov chains, but is a qualitative notion: it guarantees that path-enumeration algorithms terminate, without an a priori bound on the horizon. We study decisiveness quantitatively of Markov chains, and apply our results to the approximate quantitative coverability problem for effective probabilistic well-structured transition systems (pWSTS). We introduce truncation sets, which represent the horizons sufficient to approximate the reachability probability within a precision $\varepsilon$. These sets reformulate decisiveness quantitatively, and their elements can be computed when it is decisive. To obtain such horizons, before any exploration, we introduce geometrically reachable sets, for which the probability of not reaching them within n steps decreases exponentially in n, up to a prefactor depending on the initial state. Horizons valid for all initial states exist iff this prefactor can be chosen uniformly for boundedly coarse chains. For such pWSTS, including probabilistic vector addition systems and Galton-Watson processes, we obtain a priori global horizons growing at most logarithmically in $1/\varepsilon$. In the non-uniform case, we give a drift condition ensuring the existence of a finite geometrically reachable set. Under this condition, we derive a priori horizons growing at most logarithmically in $1/\varepsilon$ and in the weight w(x) measuring the size of the initial state x. In both cases, we compute a horizon function whose evaluation on any initial state and precision requires only a constant number of elementary operations $(+, -, \times, / \text{ and } \log)$. For probabilistic lossy channel systems, this yields, to our knowledge, the first explicit a priori horizons from arbitrary initial states, and it extends to $\nu$-pLCS, a new infinitely branching variant with probabilistic emissions.
item.dc:creator: Rapha\"el Faure, Alain Finkel, Lina Ye

item.title: The Proof-Theoretic Foundations of the Principle of Reiteration in Natural Deduction
item.description: arXiv:2610.35711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the proof-theoretic foundations of the principle of reiteration (R) in natural deduction, arguing that its legitimacy originates in the structural preservation of formulae within sequent calculus rather than in an independent logical rule. By examining singlesuccedent and multisuccedent sequent calculus, we demonstrate how logical operations transform principal formulae while preserving unaffected antecedent and succedent contexts. We subsequently analyse the schematic formulation of reiteration and compare natural deduction derivations with corresponding sequent calculus derivations. This comparison identifies two fundamental functions of reiteration, namely the reuse of previously employed formulae and the restoration of previously derived conclusions. We conclude that reiteration introduces no independent inferential content but explicitly represents the structural continuity of inferential dependencies already included into sequent calculus.
item.dc:creator: Khashayar Irani

item.title: The Undecidability of FO3 and the Calculus of Relations with Just One Binary Relation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The validity problem for first-order logic is a well-known undecidable problem. The undecidability also holds even for $\mathsf{FO}3$ and (equational formulas of) the calculus of relations. In this paper we tighten these undecidability results to the following: (1) $\mathsf{FO}3$ with just one binary relation is undecidable even without equality; and (2) the calculus of relations with just one character and with only composition, union, and complement is undecidable. Additionally we prove that the finite validity problem is also undecidable for the above two classes.
item.dc:creator: Yoshiki Nakamura

item.title: Two Uncertainties Are Not One: Disagreement versus Decision-Risk in Cheap Structured Content Moderation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Content moderation compresses a graded, contested human judgment into a binary act (leave up / take down) over billions of items, at a scale where running a frontier LLM on every post is uneconomical. A new class of frozen "System One" models returns typed, calibrated decisions instead of text at ~USD 0.000025 per call and ~100 ms. We run the first independent audit of one such model on 142,658 human-labeled comments, and benchmark it against 14 frontier reasoning models (the GPT-5.x, Claude, Gemini 3, and Grok families) on a shared probe set. Two findings stand out. First, the cheap model is accuracy-competitive: its zero-shot classification AUROC (0.83) is not statistically separable (paired bootstrap, n=56; a failure to reject parity, not proof of equivalence) from 13 of the 14 frontier systems while costing 1-3 orders of magnitude less, and it is no worse calibrated than several of them. Second, "confidence" conflates two uncertainties that come apart: human disagreement (where annotators split on satire and coded language) and decision risk (where the automatic action is costly-wrong). Under an asymmetric moderation loss these call for opposite escalation signals, so no single confidence number serves both. Because the model prices extra questions at nearly zero, decomposing the judgment into parallel sub-questions and reading their spread recovers a human-disagreement signal that the model's native confidence misses -- but this remedy is specific: it helps the weakest, disagreement-blind models and only when the decomposition aligns with the sources of disagreement; a specialist toxicity model and the strongest LLMs do not need it, and the effect is distribution-sensitive. We will release the instrument, the cached runs, and the analysis.
item.dc:creator: Karan Yadav

item.title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
item.description: arXiv:2610.33860v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user present. We describe the development of Fuse throughout 2026, as it moved from a prescribed pipeline of agents paced by human review to an orchestrator that dispatches specialists, provers, and parallel children on its own. We designed for this shift, keeping project state, tooling, and interface design separate from orchestration so that agents could take over more of the work as models improved. We report Fuse's use in a formalization of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and a study of prover models. We close with lessons for the next generation of autoformalization systems. Fuse Desktop, an open-source local version, is available at https://github.com/project-numina/fuse-desktop.
item.dc:creator: Justin Asher, Yichuan Cao, Ruichen Qiu, Pietro Pellegrino, Jia Li

item.title: Meta-Mathematics of Algebraic Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2610.33938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We initiate the study of the meta-mathematics of algebraic circuit lower bounds, aiming both to gain insight into the methods sufficient and necessary to prove algebraic circuit lower bounds, and to contribute to the study of bounded arithmetic as a logical foundation for complexity lower bounds. We demonstrate that while algebraic circuit lower bounds are hard for somewhat weak proof systems such as Polynomial Calculus Resolution ($\mathsf{PCR}$), contemporary lower bounds are efficiently provable in proof systems and bounded arithmetic theories corresponding to $\mathsf{NC}^2$, such as $\mathsf{VNC}^2$ and the corresponding class of propositional Frege proofs of quasipolynomial-size. Moreover, going below $\mathsf{VNC}^2$ into algebraic constant-depth reasoning is likely insufficient to efficiently prove already constant-depth algebraic circuit lower bounds. Under an algebraic analogue of the Krajicek--Razborov conjecture, our results suggest that proving superpolynomial lower bounds for general algebraic circuits will require stronger reasoning than that used in the rank-based proofs studied here. Specifically, we show the following.
item.dc:creator: Michal Garlik, Svyatoslav Gryaznov, Jiaqi Lu, Rahul Santhanam, Iddo Tzameret

item.title: Propositional formula minimization is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete under many-one reductions
item.description: arXiv:2610.34516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Minimum Equivalent Expression problem (MEE) asks, given a propositional formula $\phi$ and an integer $k$, whether $\phi$ is equivalent to a formula with at most $k$ occurrences of propositional variables. While the problem is clearly in $\Sigma_2^p$, its completeness under polynomial-time many-one reductions has remained open since at least 1979. Buchfuhrer and Umans showed in 2008 that it is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions. In this note, we present a proof discovered by GPT-Sol-6.1 which establishes that MEE is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete also under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
item.dc:creator: Reijo Jaakkola

item.title: Inductive Grounded Arithmetic: Goodstein, the Hydra, and $\Gamma_0$
item.description: arXiv:2610.34548v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: What does a recursive definition mean when the logic is grounded, so a sentence is true only if a terminating process makes it so? Kripke's answer for the special case of truth was the least fixed point. This paper takes that answer as a rule. Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) already writes any recursive definition as one self-referential term, paradoxes included. Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA) adds the elimination rule for every positive one, so that accessibility, the winning positions of a game, and grounded truth itself each come with their own induction principle. The rule is sound for the omega model and the system is consistent, both machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL. With the rule, IGA proves Goodstein's theorem outright, in a logic without implication at an undecided hypothesis, and the Kirby-Paris hydra game for primitive recursive strategies, both with every step of the arithmetic a grounded derivation. It proves the Cantor normal forms well-founded, from which the well-foundedness of the standard $\varepsilon_0$ notation system in HOL follows, and it certifies the Veblen notation as an ordinal below every $\varphi(n,0)$. It defines Kripke truth for RGA's own language as one fixed point that agrees with the omega model exactly. Two equivalences locate what the classical world has and the grounded one does not. IGA proves the whole Veblen notation well-founded exactly when it admits bivalence of accessibility for that order, and bivalence of accessibility for an order is sound exactly when the order is well-founded; so $\Gamma_0$ lies at most one instance of excluded middle away, at the accessibility predicate of the notation, and that instance, the well-foundedness sentence and one membership claim in a primitive-recursive form of Kleene's $\mathcal O$ are interderivable over IGA.
item.dc:creator: Bryan Ford

item.title: SoK: Timestamps Are Not a Time Model: Rethinking Temporal Reasoning in Host-Based Intrusion Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.35151v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Host-based intrusion detectors order events, window audit streams and sequence attack stages by their timestamps. Every conclusion they draw therefore rests on assumptions about clocks, delivery, entity identity and the integrity of the evidence, and most of these assumptions go unstated. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) makes them explicit. Drawing on temporal databases, stream processing and runtime verification, we distill five components of a time model, together with a checklist of evidence assumptions and four levels of guarantee, and walk through a running campaign with them. A documented search yields fifteen families of detection and investigation. For papers selected by screening role and period, plus named systems and landmarks, we check the stated assumptions in the full texts, and we assess eleven temporal knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) formalisms and a learned baseline on nine attack patterns. Some early alert correlators stated clock and delivery assumptions, and forensics measures clock error. Current provenance-based detectors state no clock bound. Four audited papers describe input-ordering conditions or conventions, but none specifies conditions for conclusion validity across a stated class of delivery failures. In the selected provenance-based systems, campaign composition uses system-specific procedures or objectives, learned state, causal graph queries or language models, and beyond CEP-based query systems, we found no temporal rule language or stream reasoner from KRR applied to host audit data. In 28 of 38 audited provenance-era detector papers, capture or stored evidence is trusted or its manipulation is placed out of scope, and none says which conclusions survive deleted, delayed or forged records. Five open challenges follow from these gaps.
item.dc:creator: Rene Heinzl, Markus Nissl

item.title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
item.description: arXiv:2610.35523v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but constructing them manually is challenging and requires substantial expertise. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework which follows the generate-verify-refine paradigm and tightly integrates LLMs with symbolic verification. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a code-completion task by inserting placeholders into the input program and constraining the LLM to fill four predefined slots for each loop. The completed program is then checked by a symbolic verifier. If verification succeeds, a valid ranking function is obtained; otherwise, the verifier's diagnostics are translated into natural-language feedback that guides iterative refinement of the LLM's output. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using MiniMax V2.7, RAINFALL synthesizes verifiable ranking functions for 323 programs (90.22%), outperforming all promising baselines. In particular, it solves 12 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the best-performing baseline and winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination category. Furthermore, combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 increases the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs). We also conduct ablation study confirming individual contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic information feedback. Experiments across LLMs further confirm the effectiveness of RAINFALL. Our results suggest a generic, sound framework for ranking-function synthesis and, beyond termination, LLM-assisted synthesis of formally checkable liveness certificates, both of which represent new directions of software engineering research.
item.dc:creator: Rongkang Li, Jiaxin Hu, Taolue Chen, Yong Li, Fu Song, Zhilin Wu

item.title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.35596v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Papers in statistical theory rest on long proofs that few readers check line by line. We present KAPPA (Kit of Agents for Proof-checking Papers with a proof Assistant), open-source software that organizes language model agents, run by Claude Code, to translate the proofs of a LaTeX paper into the proof assistant Lean 4 with its library Mathlib and check them there, result by result. Each numbered result receives one of four verdicts: verified unconditionally; verified conditionally, with every cited or unproved input stated as a named hypothesis; issue recorded, with its place in the paper and the side at fault; or unfinished, with the reason. The kit follows the paper's own proof step by step, rather than finding a new one. Separate agents write and review, each statement is compared with the paper before it is proved and fingerprinted afterwards, and every verdict rests on evidence that can be rerun without a language model. The kit runs unattended for hours, waits out usage limits, re-checks only what a revision changed and reports its cost by role, model and result. We describe the design, walk through a complete run, and apply the kit to four example papers with answer keys and to three published statistical papers, checked blind in their versions from before public corrections. In all three, the kit found the published error at the step that the correction names, together with further problems that we confirmed by hand. Given the same papers directly, the same language model working with Lean classified fewer results correctly on the longest paper and reported some statements narrower than the paper's as proved; no verdict of the kit claimed more than its Lean evidence showed.
item.dc:creator: Zihua She, Xiao Wang

item.title: The Complexity of Data-Free Nfer
item.description: arXiv:2407.03155v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nfer is a Runtime Verification language for the analysis of event traces that applies rules to create hierarchies of time intervals. This work examines the complexity of the evaluation and satisfiability problems for the data-free fragment of nfer. The evaluation problem asks whether a given interval is generated by applying rules to a known input, while the satisfiability problem asks if an input exists that will generate a given interval. By excluding data from the language, we obtain polynomial-time algorithms for the evaluation problem and for satisfiability when only considering inclusive rules. Furthermore, we show decidability for the satisfiability problem for cycle-free specifications with a NExpTime lower bound and undecidability for satisfiability of full data-free nfer.
item.dc:creator: Sean Kauffman, Kim Guldstrand Larsen, Martin Zimmermann

item.title: The Qualitative Collapse of Concurrent Games (Extended Version)
item.description:
arXiv:2410.11389v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we construct an interpretation-preserving functor from a category of concurrent games to the category of Scott domains and Scott-continuous functions. We give a concrete description of this functor, extending earlier results on the relational collapse of game semantics. The crux is an intricate combinatorial lemma allowing us to synchronize states of strategies which reach the same resources, but with different multiplicity.
Putting this together with the previously established relational collapse, this provides a new proof of the qualitative-quantitative correspondence first established by Ehrhard in his celebrated extensional collapse theorem. Whereas Ehrhard's proof is indirect and rests on an abstract realizability construction, our result gives a concrete, combinatorial description of the extraction of quantitative information from a qualitative model.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Clairambault

item.title: A meta-modal logic for bisimulations
item.description: arXiv:2507.15117v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a novel modal study of bisimulations. Our contribution is threefold. First, we extend the basic modal language with a new modality $\nbi$, whose intended meaning is universal quantification over all states that are bisimilar to the current one under a given bisimulation. We show that bisimulations are definable in this object language via frame validity (for the forth and back conditions) and model validity (for the atomic harmony condition). Additionally, some other related notions (refinements, simulations, bisimulations for a restricted set of variables, and $n$-bisimulations) are also shown to be definable. Second, we provide a sound and complete axiomatisation of the class of all pairs of Kripke models that are bisimulation-related. Third, we show that the satisfiability problem of this logic is decidable and PSPACE-complete via a translation to standard modal logic $K$ under a simple frame condition. All our results are encoded and verified by Isabelle/HOL.
item.dc:creator: Alfredo Burrieza, Fernando Soler-Toscano, Antonio Yuste-Ginel

item.title: Case Studies in Generalized Kantorovich-Rubinstein Duality
item.description: arXiv:2510.23552v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The classical Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality guarantees coincidence between metrics on the space of probability distributions defined on the one hand via transport plans (couplings) and on the other hand via price functions. Both constructions have been lifted to the level of generality of set functors, with the construction based on couplings referred to as the Wasserstein or simply the coupling-based lifting, and the price-function-based construction as the Kantorovich or codensity lifting, both based on a choice of quantitative modalities for the given functor. It is known that every coupling-based lifting can be expressed as a price-function-based lifting; however, the latter in general needs to use additional modalities. We give an example showing that this cannot be avoided in general. We refer to cases in which the same modalities can be used as satisfying the generalized Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. We establish the generalized Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality in this sense for two important cases: The L\'evy-Prokhorov distance on distributions, which finds wide-spread applications in machine learning due to its favourable stability properties, and the standard metric on convex sets of distributions that arises by combining the Hausdorff and Kantorovich-Rubinstein distances. Furthermore we generalize (coupling-based) functor liftings from set functors to functors which act on (pseudo-)metric spaces, thus incorporating new example functors that map to closed subsets respectively Radon measures.
item.dc:creator: Paul Wild, Lutz Schr\"oder, Pedro Nora, Barbara K\"onig, Jonas Forster

item.title: Interaction Improvement
item.description: arXiv:2601.01638v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The relational semantics of linear logic is a powerful framework for defining resource-aware models of the $\lambda$-calculus. However, its quantitative aspects are not reflected in the preorders and equational theories induced by these models. Indeed, they can be characterized in terms of (in)equalities between B\"ohm trees up to extensionality, which are qualitative in nature. We employ the recently introduced checkers calculus to define a quantitative contextual preorder on $\lambda$-terms, and demonstrate that it coincides with the preorder associated to the relational semantics.
item.dc:creator: Adrienne Lancelot, Giulio Manzonetto, Guy McCusker, Gabriele Vanoni

item.title: Partial Rewriting and Value Interpretation of Logically Constrained Terms (Full Version)
item.description: arXiv:2601.22191v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Logically constrained term rewrite systems (LCTRSs) are a rewriting formalism that naturally supports built-in data structures, including integers and bit-vectors. The recent framework of existentially constrained terms and most general constrained rewriting on them (Takahata et al., 2025) has many advantages over the original approach of rewriting constrained terms. In this paper, we introduce partial constrained rewriting, a variant of rewriting existentially constrained terms whose underlying idea has already appeared implicitly in previous analyses and applications of LCTRSs. We examine the differences between these two notions of constrained rewriting. First, we establish a direct correspondence between them, leveraging subsumption and equivalence of constrained terms where appropriate. Then we give characterizations of each of them, using the interpretation of existentially constrained terms by instantiation. We further introduce the novel notion of value interpretation, that highlights subtle differences between partial and most general rewriting.
item.dc:creator: Takahito Aoto, Naoki Nishida, Jonas Sch\"opf

item.title: Dynamic Planar Graph Isomorphism is in DynFO
item.description: arXiv:2604.22365v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Consider two planar graphs which are subject to edge insertions and deletions. We show that whether the two graphs are isomorphic can be maintained with first-order logic formulas and auxiliary data of polynomial size. This places the dynamic planar graph isomorphism problem into the dynamic descriptive complexity class DynFO. As a consequence, there is a dynamic constant-time parallel algorithm with polynomial-size auxiliary data which maintains whether two dynamic planar graphs are isomorphic.
item.dc:creator: Samir Datta, Asif Khan, Felix Tschirbs, Nils Vortmeier, Thomas Zeume

item.title: Goedel Logics: On the Elimination of The Absoluteness Operator
item.description: arXiv:2605.05016v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the eliminability of the absoluteness operator Delta in Goedel logics. While Delta is not definable from the standard connectives and disrupts important proof-theoretic properties, we show that it becomes eliminable at the propositional level under a non-standard semantics in which all propositional atoms (except the truth constant 'True') are interpreted strictly below 1. Under this semantics, every formula containing Delta is equivalent to a disjunction of chain formulas, yielding a Delta-free normal form (standard and non-standard semantics coincide w.r.t. valid formulas without Delta). We further analyze the situation in the first-order setting, where Delta-elimination fails in general due to recursion-theoretic and topological constraints, but can be recovered under witnessed semantics.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Baaz, Mariami Gamsakhurdia

item.title: A note reviewing Turing's 1936
item.description: arXiv:1308.0497v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: By closely rereading the original Turing's 1936 article, we can gain insight about that it is based on the claim to have defined a number which is not computable, arguing that there can be no machine computing the diagonal on the enumeration of the computable sequences. This article provides a careful analysis of Turing's original argument, demonstrating that it cannot be regarded as a conclusive proof. Furthermore, it shows that there is no evidence supporting the existence of a defined number that is not computable.
item.dc:creator: Paola Cattabriga

item.title: A categorical formulation of Kraus' paradox
item.description: arXiv:2403.17961v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a categorical formulation of Kraus' "magic trick" for recovering information from truncated types. Rather than type theory, we work in Van den Berg-Moerdijk path categories with a univalent universe, and rather than propositional truncation we work with arbitrary cofibrations, which includes truncation as a special case. We show, using Kraus' argument that any cofibration with homogeneous domain is a monomorphism. We give some simple concrete examples in groupoids to illustrate the interaction between homogeneous types, cofibrations and univalent fibrations.
item.dc:creator: Andrew W. Swan

item.title: EntailLLM: Verifying Agent-Generated Vulnerability Discovery Paths with Domain Knowledge via Logic Programming
item.description: arXiv:2608.01763v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly used to analyze potential software vulnerabilities, but their outputs can silently violate domain knowledge, limiting their reliability in safety-critical settings such as medical devices. Prior work either treats that output as a prediction to be scored or constrains it to walks within a single knowledge graph; neither checks whether reasoning over a binary is entailed by an independent body of domain knowledge. We present EntailLLM, a framework that includes a specialized LLM agent and a validation mechanism. The agent proposes a traversal path of the function call graph for a vulnerability, which is checked against a separate knowledge graph and a logic program by an entailment procedure under annotated logic. We evaluate EntailLLM by examining six specialized agents across three CWE classes, and eight binaries varying in size from 405 to 12,696 functions. The agents improve pooled entailment from 77% to 98%, with entailment decreasing in only 3 of 118 configurations. We found that the best-performing agent combines self-refinement and a priori domain knowledge. EntailLLM is deployed end-to-end on real medical-device binaries, reaching 98% pooled entailment without per-device tuning. Our framework inherits the formal guarantees of generalized annotated logic, providing logical verification of agent output that is both explainable and grounded in well-defined semantics.
item.dc:creator: Kaustuv Mukherji, Jaikrishna Manojkumar Patil, Colton Payne, Paulo Shakarian, Dana Warmsley, Nigel Stepp, Evelyn Kim

item.title: Internal Reasoning and Consistency in Reflective Grounded Arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2608.16140v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) is a paracomplete arithmetic allowing direct expression of any general-recursive computation. Every RGA term is a program and truth is grounded evaluation, with a proof certificate at each universal quantifier. This paper shows, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development, that such a system is powerful enough to carry out its own metamathematics. A fuel-indexed decider of RGA's grounded semantics and checkers for RGA's proofs are compiled primitive-recursive RGA terms. RGA proves internally that its decider never affirms $0 = 1$, and that every well-formed term it affirms has an RGA proof accepted by a transparent test. RGA proves that, for each valid RGA proof, its conclusion is true. RGA proves that each grounded-true well-formed term is provable. RGA proves that no proof in either of two decided classes of RGA proofs derives $0 = 1$. G\"odel's incompleteness theorems hold for RGA, but their proofs must be adapted. In RGA an implication $A \rightarrow B$ is strictly stronger than an entailment $A \vdash B$: RGA discharges a hypothesis only when it can prove the hypothesis decided, a restriction needed to defuse Curry's paradox. RGA's implication is material and RGA has the disjunction property, so RGA proves no implication between ungrounded sentences. The implications that the textbook proof of G\"odel's second theorem uses are of this kind and fail, but the entailments and rules it uses hold: G\"odel's proof survives as entailments. RGA does not prove its consistency sentence $\mathit{Con}$: RGA carries out G\"odel's argument internally, with a decided proof predicate and explicit proof transformers, and only the last step, that RGA does not prove $0 = 1$, is left to HOL. RGA also proves its own second incompleteness theorem as an entailment from $\mathit{Con}$, and as a single sentence quantified over proofs.
item.dc:creator: Bryan Ford

item.title: A Degree--Size Relation for Resolution over Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2610.00837v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For every constant-width CNF, we show that linear degree in polynomial calculus (PC) implies exponential size in resolution over constant-degree polynomials, over the same prime field. Applications include exponential lower bounds for CNFs in $\operatorname{Res}(\operatorname{PC}_r/\mathbb{F}_p)$ and hence in $\operatorname{Res}(\oplus_p)$, separations between different moduli, improved lower bounds for $\operatorname{Res}(k)$ up to $k=\varepsilon\log n$, proof-search consequences, and an implication of super-polynomial $AC^0[p]$-Frege bounds from very strong PC degree lower bounds. The proof uses the common-multiplier idea isolated from Braun [arXiv:2609.23015] to construct a Razborov--Smolensky approximation that preserves inferences, without introducing extension variables. The approximation errors are measured by ranks of the multiplication maps induced by the error-witness polynomials, modulo bounded-degree PC consequences.
item.dc:creator: Shuo Pang

item.title: Machine-Checked Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates
item.description: arXiv:2610.05335v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Proofs of authenticated-data-structure updates built on the Goldwasser-Kalai-Rothblum (GKR) protocol are sound only if three arguments hold together: the soundness of the protocol, the exactness of the arithmetization that turns an update into a circuit, and the binding of the hash commitments. For GKR, the mechanizations we know of stop at the sumcheck subprotocol. For sparse-Merkle membership, non-membership and update as compiled by the StateSync-GKR prover, we machine-check in Isabelle/HOL the first two arguments, their composition, and the leaf side of the third. For layered circuits with linear, product and cube gates, the cube gate serving the $x^3$ S-box of Poseidon2, we prove that for a false output claim, the event that some layer's sumcheck accepts a false sum while all earlier carried claims are false has probability at most $(s_{\mathrm{out}} + \sum_i (2 s_i d_i + 1))/|\mathbb{F}|$, where layer $i$ has $2^{s_i}$ wires and $d_i$ bounds the degree of its sumcheck polynomial. We instantiate the bound over the exact quartic extension of the 31-bit KoalaBear field from which small-field provers draw challenges, so that the denominator is $p^4 \approx 2^{124}$, and lift base-field layers and false outputs into it. In a constraint-level model of the compiler, with the hash sub-circuits as abstract functions, the verifier model accepts exactly the valid transitions, and leaf-commitment collisions reduce to sponge collisions. Their composition is mechanized for claims that no witness makes valid, and from the mechanized theorems it follows on paper that the bad event has probability at most this bound for every input that does not encode a valid transition. All bounds concern the interactive public-coin protocol with uniform challenges; the Fiat-Shamir transformation, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge are outside the model.
item.dc:creator: Jinwook Kim
